title: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams Interview, 1967-05-13
interviewee: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams

blocks.x: Okay, we got the second reel of James Butch Cage on May the 13th, 1967. What do you want to say now? What do you want to say?

My mama used to have one song called Black Nigga Baby, Black Feet and Shiny Eyes, Black all over in the bone the other way with any rubber feet. And they turn that nigga around and knock him in the head and the white folks say you got to kill the nigga dead.
What was that, was the song?

That was the song? That's the song. Some white folks, they'd hug him in the flinty, some don't get so fat, my Danny. I want to take a dagger, eat the meat and chew the grizzles, get up in the morning and be free.
That must be from Slavery Time. It is. You must know plenty of songs from Slavery Time. Oh I do, that's all I know. Did you ever cut any cane?

Oh yes, I was a pretty good butcher for cane. I'd ruin more than I cut. You'd ruin more than you cut? I ain't been on a cane before I've been in pain. Cut it too short, you know. Too long and leaves. I used to go ever, you know. I used to go ever fall. Low top and high bottom, huh? Yes, when I cut it low bottom, top.
That's what I mean. Low top and high bottom when you cut it. Did you sing when you cut cane?
Sometimes I sang. Sometimes I wasn't just going. I'd be raising more or less trying to keep up. You know, if you get behind, I'd have to put a band on you. The boys and I'd stand right over you.
Where was this at? That's in Smithfield. In where? Smithfield. Is that nearby? I want to tell you from Baton Rouge. Oh yeah.
It's across the river from Baton Rouge, twelve miles north.
North of Port Allen? Yeah. I think I know where it is.
I used to go to different places. I'm at the Wildwood.
Napoleonville.
Napoleonville. He know them.
Where?
He know them. He know them. Yes.

And you always, you cut cane out there? Yes, yes. Well you were a grown man then, huh? Oh yes. You couldn't keep up, you couldn't keep up with me. I'm a grown man. I'm a grown man. I'm a grown man. I'm a grown man. You couldn't keep up though, huh? Well I could keep up.
I'd keep fast up. I'd get way up in there so the man wouldn't follow me. That's the reason I didn't cut it good all the time.
Well you just, he wanted you to tighten up, huh?
When I tightened up, I wasn't half cut it. Yeah. Well then, I'll get up in there and cut it right. Mm-hmm. I see.

Do you want to ask some questions? I'm running out of questions, you know. You are. Well. Now did you, I don't know. I don't have any questions. Really. You know that first song you played when we came here? Yeah. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Remember that?
Yeah. That's You Don't Know My Mind.
Oh yeah. I heard a record of that by a guy named Henry Sims I think. Did you ever hear of him?
No, I didn't know where you are then, but I used to play that all the time.
Yeah, I guess it went around sort of.
You know, when they see me laughing, I'm laughing, and they keep from crying.
Yeah. Did you have a box to play records on when you were growing up ever? No, sir. I mean one of those old wind up boxes around you. Yeah, sir.
Didn't have no music box, nothing. They had one made like a cane, just like the bill cane. It rolled around.
Like a cup, yeah. Yeah. Called it a cylinder, that's what they call it. Yeah. I was the Jews. Do you remember the names of any of the records you used to listen to, different people you used to like?
Like you say, you like a man like I like a you. We all, we all both like the same.
This very day, I'd like to say, I'd like to change your name. Yeah. I remember that.
Why don't you come home, Bill Bailey?
Oh yeah? Yeah.
Oh, I like that. I'm a whole piece. Did you listen to any... Please don't let me fall. What's that? Babe, please don't let me fall. Babe, please don't let me fall.
I don't know that one. Who did that? Boys, boys, don't let me fall.

Y'all are the changes. Boys, boys, don't let me fall. Who did that? Who sang that? Oh, anybody, you know. Anybody could sing it. That's a good song. I just wondered if you listen to any blues singers on records.
Yes, I listened to all of them.
Who did you listen to? I listened to Blind and that one's Jefferson. You know him? I got his records. Blind Lemon, huh? Yes. I got his records.
I got the Black Snake Mawn. Yes. I listened to Besser Smith from the Black Snake Mawn. I listened to Besser Smith from the Black Snake Mawn.
I listened to Besser Smith from the Black Snake Mawn. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I don't want no more. Bessie Smith.

Yeah. I know about her. I got her records too. Yeah, sir. See, I keep all that, you know, because I figure that's going a hundred years from now, people will still be looking for records by Bessie Smith and Blind Lemon. Yeah, sir. So we'll keep all that. Yeah, what other records do you remember? And what other people are at this time?
I'm trying to say something now. I remember Mama Rainey. Oh, yeah.
I like her. Did you ever see her?
No, sir. I saw a lot of them up there, and I forgot what they call her. She's got to play like Mama. She can't get off.
Was she about the same, about as big as Memphis Minnie? Yeah, yeah. About like Memphis Minnie, a big woman? Yeah.
She got on the stage and she saw her.
Did you ever see Memphis Minnie? No. What I see, they shot noises here, a big woman.
Mm-hmm. No, I forgot what they call her. You hear the thing about Mississippi. Weeping Willow Blue. The Weeping Willow?

That's Bessie Smith. I know it. Bessie Smith's like that. I know it. I know it. Bessie Smith's like that. I know it too. Yeah. Her too, huh? Yeah. Where did you see her? What town would that be? That's Newport, Rhode Island. I saw her. Oh, that's late years, huh? Yeah. I saw the one what I'm talkin' bout.
Oh, that's late years, huh? Yeah. I thought it wasn't what I'm talking about. It wasn't Ramping Ma Rainey, but it put him in the mind.

Oh, I know who he's talking about. Is it Mahaney? No, it's a white woman, huh? What's that? Is that a white woman that tries to sing like Ma Rainey in them? No, she was calling. Oh, I don't know who it would be then. Why are there so many of them?

I don't remember that song about if you're broken hearted and your man is out of town, go to the river and jump right up. Take your chance. Take your chance. Take your chance. Make Mennowiller. If he don't come back, let me tell you what to do. Jump right up with boys, cause you ain't no more than you. Cause I thought my man would kiss him morning, noon, and night. I'd wipe you clothes and keep you clean, try to treat him right. Then he went and left me after all I tried to do. The way he treated you, he'd do the same. Mainly he'd do the same to you. I was weeping forever.

I used to play that. I like that. Punch Miller still plays that down in New Orleans. Yes. You might have heard him. He was a solid screen for a long time. Yes. I was born. I ain't been far. Yeah. What about your, uh, back to your family. Now you say your mother was a dancer.
Yes, she was the best. And frankly, God, anybody that doesn't know. And your father?
He was, he didn't dance. He didn't dance, huh? No. And your brothers, now let's go, and your sisters, did they play any music or dance?

Yes, my sister played cardine, both of them. I had two. And I had one brother playing cardine. And are they living? Oh, no, I don't know. Right here. You haven't heard from them, any of them? And thirteen had on.
Thirteen?
Yes. And I don't know what now they had.
Well, you know Tuesday and you know Lloyd Brad. I don't know what that is. There's so many more. You know what Fred is playing guitar.
Fred was a guitar player.
And he had a son, he's a guitar player.
I've got a boy that plays guitar.

Does he live in Syracuse? Yes. You told me about him once before, I think. Yes. You got his address up there? Yes, we got it. I'd like to get that from him because I have a friend who teaches up there. He might get him a little job in Syracuse. He's one of the head men at the school up there. Yes, yes, yes. Hey, when you were like growing up and stuff, you didn't hear things like trumpets and stuff like that, or did you?
No. You didn't?
You had a church. Each way, you're going to church.
I was going to be as good as you couldn't get.
You couldn't get them, huh?
No, we wasn't able to get, we did get some drums. Why, my brother, be making fun. Be ordering some drums.

Well, when you went into town, what kind of music did they have there? Why did you meet? Well, you say you lived out in the country, huh? Yes. But I mean, like, if you went into Meadville, did they ever have a show there with a band? With trombones and cornets? Oh, no.
After the dead, they didn't lie you in there.

They didn't lie you in. No, the white people, they had that. Well, I thought maybe they had it out on the street sometimes, you know. Sometimes you see them marching up and down the street here. No, but Meadville, they don't fly it no, huh? It's a tiny town, huh? Yeah. What about in Natchez? Natchez is a good size little town. Well, did you see any bands marching up and down the streets? Yeah, sir. I thought some of them died. What would they do that for? Would it be for a holiday or for a show or for what?
Yeah, for different things like that.
Yeah, sir.
They used to beat drums when people died, too. When people died, they beat drums. Yeah, they're nothing.
Did they have anything besides drums when people died?
No, I don't think they did. Drums are the whole time standby.
How would they beat the drums? They would beat them on the way, taking them? Where would they beat the drums?
I beat them going to the cemetery and coming back.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Would that be any society or a lodge or a lot? Something like that, yeah. Something like that, huh? Yeah. Did you ever belong to any societies yourself? No more than I belong to that and all that. The masons across the street? Oh, no. What society is that over there? It's a benevolent. Call itself what it ain't. Call itself which? Monelent. Monelent. We'll look at it when we go across so we can get it down straight. We'll write it down.
It's a benevolent side. We belong to it. Mm-hmm. Benevolent?
Benevolent. Yeah. But it must have a name, huh? Just benevolent. That's the name of it. Benevolent is there. Yeah.
Well, it ain't what it say. Not all the way.

I can't see it from here. It ain't on there. Ruth. Ruth chapter of something. Friend accepted masons, I think. There's a right one on there. That's a Masonic, huh, over there? Yeah. That's a Masonic. That's a Masonic hall over there. Yeah.
Masonic and benevolent together.

Yeah, they give you sick benefits? No. We don't belong. Oh, yeah. That's too little to talk about. Oh, yeah. You don't belong to it. I see. We belong to the benevolent. Oh, yeah. That's all right. Yeah, but the benevolent. But they don't belong to the man. Do they give you sick benefits?
If you stay in the bed or over there, they give you $2.50 a week.
$2.50 a week.
Yeah.
And you're supposed to buy your food out of that, I guess.
I mean, I'll say that over now.
Yeah. They don't give you anything, huh? No. They charge you, though, I bet. Oh, that's right. That's right. How much does it cost to belong?
We pay. I don't know what I paid now to get down, but I've been in there so long. We pay $0.50 every time a member die. And we have $2.50 if the dog die every month.

Yeah. And they tax you. It's like a tax, they call it, a member die. I know what you're talking about. I see how it works. Dick, you got anything you want to ask? Yeah, I want to ask. I don't really know what questions you've asked before.
No, don't worry about it.
I want to ask you when it was you used to hear him play drums when someone died. When was that about?
When it was?
Yeah, when. About when?
Well, between 1909 and five. 1905 and nine.
They kind of quit it after that? They didn't do it? I mean, did you hear it after 1909?
Not much. They used to hear it when they go around these towns.
Yeah.
They could hear it in the country a little poor day.
They never had the fife with the drums.
Yes, ma'am. That's all that music they had.

Oh, I see. Would they have the fife and the drums when somebody died? Yes, ma'am. They would? Hey, fair. What would they play when somebody died? They must have played some kind of... Let's go down in Jordan. Let's go down in Jordan. It's all over what Jordan is. Up in Memphis, he said they played Nero My God to Thee. Yeah. I hear a lot of different ones. Yeah, they played different songs. Yeah. Yeah.
Good.

Somebody caught it. Somebody outside? We can turn it off. Somebody caught it. I'll put you on. I'll put you on. One more question. Uh... Do you know if any young kids are going to take up that same color fiddling you play? Do you think any of those kids will ever do the same as you?
Not many of them.

Not many of them. They may find them going to school. It's pretty good sometimes. But they can't play that real dance music, huh? Not those old-time numbers. I haven't heard... Oh, but they play something else. They play something else. They like the new music now. Yeah. I never do hear any of them. You know, I used to hear... When I grew up in Georgia, out in the country, I used to hear plenty of fiddle players and banjo pickers. Well, nobody played that up here with... He's the only one. ...and he's fast with you. Yeah. He's the only one I ever know. I've been here 53 years. I ain't never hear nobody play. We ought to get everybody's name down who's here. Yeah. You got new people. Let's see. What's your name? We might as well start with him. We got your name. Pete, you want to tell him? Robert Pete Williams. And can we get your name, Miss Kay? Robert Pete Williams. Robert Pete Williams. Robert Pete Williams. Robert Pete Williams. Robert Pete Williams. And you're... Dick Cook. Alan or Ellen. Say, man, do you want to put your name down? No, you don't give me... I, Hickenbottom. Hickenbottom. Hickenbottom. Hickenbottom. And your first name? I. I. All right. My name is Dick Allen. So we got everybody's name down in case we all talk at once. I don't know who's who. But... You got anything else you want to tell the young students when they come to study music at the university? Me? Yeah. You want to tell them how to play?
No, they don't play my kind.

They don't play your kind. They play rock and roll now. I've never heard of rock and roll violin. Well, a friend of mine used to tell you. That old stuff he played. That new with the youngsters right now. I guess we can talk to Robert Pete Williams for a little while then. How many fingers do you pick with? I was wondering, you know. You picked it.
I only have picked with my dog finger, the stomach, which would be one finger in my thumb. But my left hand, I use all of my fingers.
You use two finger picking? Yes, sir.
Two fingers picking.
With your right hand? With my right hand. Oh, yeah. And my left hand, I use them all.
You use them all. I see.
Do you ever use three finger picking or not?
No, so I never did use three fingers. Mm-hmm. I only use two.
How many different kind of tunings do you use?
Well, I can play C, flat E, minor, Spanish.
And Spanish. Yes, sir. What is flat E, minor? Is that something open?

Well, it's an open chord. Flat E, minor, open chord, just like the Spanish. Open. Yeah. Well, that's the way I play. Now, you can take flat chord, E, minor, in Spanish. You can play that with your fingers or a knife, bow, you know. Pick.
You ever use a knife or a bottle of anger?
Yes, I have used a knife to play with. But not as much as I did my fingers. I have a four of my fingers, picking my fingers.
Do you ever use Vasterpool tuning? Ever use what they call Vasterpool?
Oh, no, sir, I didn't. Cross note? Well, when you got any cross note, when you say that flat E, minor, that's cross note.
Same as cross note, I see.

That's same as cross note. What about you? But my red playing tune is in C and Natchez. Yes. Which I can take C and Natchez and set that pick on it. And this cross note on over, just like it ain't C and Natchez. It's like it sounds like it's in Spanish.
Yeah, I see.

And they can't hardly tell the difference. Well, that's why they always told me that they didn't see how I could do it. And my way of going, playing a guitar. So I played like Lightning Hopkins. And I watched my music back like Lion, Lemon, and Jefferson.
Mm-hmm.

Yes. So I met a lot of musicians that they just kind of carried over at the way that I played a guitar. Mm-hmm. And they wanted to learn a couple of my notes to what I was picking when I was in Los Angeles. Well, some man that plays a guitar was way over me, but they just couldn't get that card. So, otherwise, when I started out playing a guitar, it must have been long, about, I'd say, 34, anyway, when I started out. Because I used to go to many supples and watch Bush Keyes play a guitar. Before I ever know what playing a guitar was.
You were born in Zachary?

This is my home in Zachary. Mm-hmm. Yes. I don't know Mr. Anderson Place. Mm-hmm. And we moved from Zachary in 28, nearby down there to Zion City. And we've been there ever since. Well, I moved over here on there. Skyward over there. Mm-hmm. But I made it up in my mind to buy me a guitar one day. First guitar that I bought it, the string was sitting upon it so high until you had to take hand-match it down and try to get a sound out. Yeah. Yeah. A fella sold it to me for a darn my head. I gave him a darn my head for it. Well, I found a little bit of a bump in the long run until I thought I had lunch. Well, I did lunch a few notes on it, but there wasn't nothing much I could do with it. And a couple of ladies working for a white lady. As she seen I was trying to learn, she said, my boss, Madam, just got a guitar down there. And she bought her board to take music lessons. But he's not interested in you. She said, come down there, she may sell it to you. So I did do that. I went down there. It was one of those high-priced guitars. Try some of that? It was one of those high-priced guitars, you know?
That's an entorment.

That's the one you got now? No, that's not the one I got now. This was a assignment that I had. It sounded like an electric box. She sold it to me and she said, I paid, well, in that time, you could get a guitar, a cheap can, for about $50 or $60. She told me she'd pay $60 for that guitar. She said, that son of mine is not interested in you. She said, I said, for $4. She sold it to me. For $4? $4. So I'd taken that guitar and I went on, went on. I got more and more with it, you know? Which I used to then play the blues. I used to play, you know, what you call the white book music then. I was just about to forget it all. Then they'd tell me I'd run there. They'd come and get me to play for me. They'd bust their part and things like that, you know? And so from that on, I got on the blues and I was going to these country's suppers playing. Down half a night like that. And they got kind of interest in me. So I made pretty good living there. The thing was cheap then, you know? And at that time, you could take about $3 or $4 and go to the store. You couldn't pack your groceries back once you buy it in at the store. So I'd come and get plays then from Thursday to Friday, Saturday and Sunday, you know? Some of them would just, you know, just wouldn't put the price on what they got to pay me at the white folks' parties. They'd just pass their head around. Sometimes I'd get $7 or $8 out of the white folks just playing. Just passing their head around, you know? This country's suppers here, brother, kids, you know, well, they'd just set your price. Is that right? Right! Right! Right! And I'd pay you $2 or something like that. So after that night, I put my guitar aside and thought I was pre-Giant Church. I met a lot of church members who told me, say, quit playing the blues and you're Giant Church. Save your soul. When I did it, and maybe about a month, I could hear the sound of music coming to me. And then I'd go back and pick my guitar up and start back the plane. So, finally I just put it down, put it where I was for good one time, maybe about a year, and I didn't fool with it no more. But I couldn't leave it all the time. I just had to go back and get it again. Start the plane. So, when I had just let it fall, I guess you know what I'm talking about. One of those captains used to call me into the hallways. And they loved the blues, you know. And they'd play some more lonesome blues. Well, I'd go in and play them blues. And they would dial the telephone and let their family at the house listening to them. To make the blues. And they would say down there, what you having, a party or something? I'd hear them tell them on the phone, no, it's got Robert Pete Williams in there playing the blues. And they'd tell me, say, you know, good as you play a guitar. I said, you don't have no business here. He plays sad and he plays lonesome. He asked. They said, we're going to get you away from here, because you have no business here. But we can't get you away from here ourselves, like we used to could. But we'll have somebody to get you away from here. I told them I'd sure appreciate it. So, they kept me working in the field one week. And they took me out the field and they sent me to the milk dairy. And they told me, say, I'm going to send you down there. I said, but it's a mean man down there. He will hit you or he will kick you. But if you do that, say, just raise your hand and let the guards know you're coming in and come on back to the camp. I told them, yes, sir. He said, you think you can wait down there? I told them, yes, sir. I got down there to that dairy and they had cows you couldn't put the machine on. Well, I had to milk all of them by a hand. And that man be sitting in that chair. He was a mean looking man, Mr. Barney, though. How can I milk a machine? How can I milk a machine? That man sat there. He'd look at me. And when they would get up and come stand over me, I'd be wondering, what is I'm milking them right or something like that? When is he thinking hit me or kick me? So I'd get up and I'd go in to my milk, come back and get under one of the cows. I could find it when I come back in and strip them, see if I got milk dry, you know? He'd shake his head and then I got on the next cow. He said, I've seen a man milking, but I've never seen a man beat you milking a cow. He said, anytime a man can out a milking machine, I don't know what to say about it. He said, who lent you out a milking? I said, well, way back there in 29, I said, Mr. White, in a milk dairy, hired me to work for him. I said, I didn't know how to milk. I said, he lent me how to milk. Hired me to work for him for $3 a week, which is $12 a month. And I said, I've been working for him 15 years. I said, of course, he raised my wages from 12 to 20. I said, of course, you know the thing was cheap then. He said, well, you're really great. He said, I wish I had you on my phone out there. I said, you have the phone? He said, yeah. I said, what about it? He said, I went to Tash for Hope, Paris. Well, I told him, I said, I wish you could. Well, I passed on off and he had some dogs that he was raising up there on the phone, you know. And he told me, he said, Rob, you look like a good old donkey. I said, yes. He said, I want you to do something for me. I said, what's that? He said, I want you to train up my dogs. He said, well, let some of these other boys go ahead of you. And they're going to hide off and maybe get them a tree or something. Then you turn the dogs loose. Well, I do that. I run those dogs for that man. And they just, what if, you know. Leave off that. Those dogs hit that trail. They go get them a tree. Go right to that tree. Start up that tree and bark up there. So, Mr. Odom, he taken a liking to me, too. So, he told Mr. Barnard, though, that nothing happened to me down there. Because I was a quiet donkey. None of them fellas do me nothing. So, one day I run into the dogs. You know, you have to hold someone that had a belt on them, you know. Well, running through the bush, I got struck in the eye. And so, Mr. Odom come down there. He said, what's the matter with his eyes? So, Mr. Barnard told him. Well, he called me in the office. I had to be up there. He said, ain't nobody jumped on you. I told him, no, sir. He said, well, I'll tell you before, Mr. Barnard. I don't want nobody hitting on me. Nobody. He said, if they do, he said, you see me. He said, I got a brother up there in North, Louisiana. He said, I'm going to get you out of here and send you to my brother. I said, you got a good record. I killed a lot about you myself. But he didn't get a chance to get me. And man, over in Dunnip Springs, Mr. Eastley got me. Yes, sir. So, as you used to come up there, they had Mr. Austin come up there. He came up there and he actually called me, I make Family Blues. I made that Family Blues with 12th, Frank Getty. And then he actually called me to the governor of the church song. Well, I did that. When I had the church song, they carried that to the boat. And then carrying that church song to the boat, Mr. Rudolph Eastley came up there and got me. I used to tell those people all the time, I said, I won't be here long. They said, oh, man like you with a fresh life. They're talking about you ain't going to be here long, ain't been here no time. I said, just forget about that. I said, I got a man that's going to help me. Who is that man? I said, that man up there. That means Jesus Christ. Some of them had to know, they said, oh, we don't think about Jesus Christ, because it ain't no God. I've been here 20-something years and they ain't gone nowhere yet. I said, well, you all just sit here and kill one another and fight and go on. I said, I'm leaving here. Well, okay.
You came to Hunnin' Coon.
That's right, first.
You get away.
So, we got the third reel. We got Butch Cage and Robert T. Williams. And Robert T. was telling us.

So, I would tell them all the time. I said, I'm a little bit of fighting going on. They told me, no, you can't do that. You got to run away. We put the dogs in behind you. I said, no, there won't be no dogs. I said, when I leave here, I said, there's somebody coming here and get me. So, I was on the post. They gave me a gun, put my guard clothes on me. And around. So, I sat up there on the post. No, no, no, no. I never could nobody get in that post before I had it locked up. And I know it's a guard. But the shore, you got that wind blowing out there. I was sitting there, holding my gun across my lap. And something come to me and patting me on my shoulder.
That's the old woman's drink. That's not a house, huh? That's too much for me.
The woman told me, don't worry. You'll be at home with your family. Christmas.
What's your life?
Well, I jumped.
What's your life?

I jumped. Mm-hmm. And I stood up and I looked. I didn't see nobody. So, I sat back down. Something come to him again. Pat him on my shoulder. I said, don't worry. Get up and pray. I got up. Looked all the way around again. So, okay, I couldn't close my eyes because I have to watch for the line walker. He got a light one. He flashed you. He got to flash him back.
Mm-hmm.
I got on my knees. But I kept my eyes out at that runner so I could see if he's coming around the corner. So if he flashed me, I could flash him back. I got down there and prayed. Prayed.
You don't drink.
And after praying, about five minutes after I got off my knees, well, the man did come around the corner. And he flashed me and I flashed him back.
But it left me feeling good. Mm-hmm. Good.

And I was standing up on my head. It wasn't a little ahead up there. I felt it good. So, when my partner come and released me that morning. I went on to the camp and I told the boy, I said, well, I'm going to tell all you fellas something. What you got to tell us this morning? I said, I ain't going to be here with y'all long. He said, oh, man, hush that racket. You know better than that. I said, okay. I said, just watch it. Well, I pulled my clothes off and I went to bed. I lay on my face. Somebody come in and they shut me. Just as I was slumming off to sleep. Said, they want you at the office somewhere. I got him, put the clothes on, went on over to the office. Well, that's Mr. Barnett over there. He come over there to get my record at Camp H over there. Mm-hmm. Well, they said, what you got to do with his record? He ain't been here no time. He said, forget about that. How long he been here? He said, I want you the record. He said, okay, okay. Well, they give him my record. He said, oh, Robert Peake. He said, you think I'll get away from here? You know that? I said, no, sir. I didn't know it. He said, that's right. I said, I'm glad of it. He said, I'm glad of it. So, and next, well, Mr. Barnett, I mean, Mr. Rudolph Eastley came. He said, I never seen you before, and I don't know you. I don't know you by your record. He said, you got a good record. And I see you ain't nothing but a phone man. And he said, I'm going to get you on my phone. Will you go? I told him, yes, sir. The man said, well, I ain't came you today. He said, well, I'll be back a few more days to get you. Well, he did, like he said, come up in there and got me and carried me up to his place up there above Zachary. And after we got there, well, that's when we met the governor and his two friends. I had my guitar. The governor made me come on into Mr. Rudolph's daughter's house. They made coffee and gave me coffee and told me to play the guitar, and I played. And even I rode in the car with the governor. And I rode down and looked at his Mr. Rudolph Eastley's hogs, cows, and everything. And I rode down there. And ever since then, and it helped some go that I've been out. But that's the very reason I don't go nowhere now, as you all asked me, did I get any plays out? Well, I would go out and play just like if the white folks would come get me, you know, and take me out like I was playing at the LSU because there's no trouble. But like, every cause of my trouble, what I got into, I was misused for another man. That's why I was in trouble. Misused for another man. So I promised the good Lord that I wasn't going out playing for no suppers no more. And I don't do it now. They wanted me over here, see, we're back with Tash for Hope. And I told them no, we're coming. Because these fellas get to drinking that wine, and throwing balls, and ask me why you come from. It's so many people that favors you. So, you tell them why you came from with that old bleeding. And just like you and the madam over there, and you, up there was it. If somebody in New York favors you, if somebody in Newport favors you later there, if somebody in San Francisco favors you, if someone in Texas favors you, everywhere favors them. That's to be thought of. Well, that's just the way the world runs. But, I would come back on this to say this. I have seen some hard times in my days. I do know the time in 32, I mean my mother. We used to work for, my mother was getting 25 cents a day, and I was getting 50 cents. But when the weapon run out, you didn't have nothing to do. We was working for a millionaire or two. You know him, that's Mr. Hughes. Yeah, yeah, he was.
He was a millionaire.

But that's all it paid. But, I remember so that we couldn't get no work. And me and my mother would walk from Baker every day trying to get on the welfare to get help. That's right. The other way, you see, I raised up my sisters and brothers without a father. I haven't had it rough all my days. I just went out to pray so hard and I just can't stay on that music all of my days. Playing the blues, I have to give God some of myself. But, he was a great big tall white man. I want to smoke so bad I didn't know what to do. He was smoking, coming along, just dressed up. I asked him for that shovel. He said the ground beats me to the shovel. He throw it down. Throw it down? My mother was inside the welfare office and I was sitting on the outside. He didn't give me that shovel. And we didn't have the fresh nickel on us to get us a kick or nothing. So, when she got through talking to my mother, we came on back up there. We walked from Baton Rouge to Baker. That's where we were living then. That old college back there. So, we were sitting down in the restroom. I picked up a fine nickel. I said, oh, I said, mama, here's a nickel. I said, we would get us a stage plant. Had a little case. That stage plant is about that long. It carries two sides to it.
Your dad?

Yeah. I remember. We got a stage plant. I gave her one side and I kept one side. And we did. And we walked all the way back home where we stopped at my uncle's house. Well, my uncle, he used to catch crawfish, bullfrogs, Simon Carney did, and sell them. I said, well, my mother, when we stopped by there, she got a little, you know, is a borrow, not a give. But she loved me, since it's the thing to cook for my children. My aunt did it. She loved it. Then we left over there, walked and went on to the house. And I said, mother, I said, I don't know what we got to do. I said, but let her wake up, I'll get a job one day. So finally, I did work upon a job. And I had been taking care of my mother until she died. But I raised up all of my sisters and brothers without a father. I slept in barns. That's right. This man was paying me $3 a week, which was $12 a month. He told my mother, he said, I'm going to feed him. But at that time, I couldn't draw my money, you know. Back in them times, they didn't give no youngsters their money. She sent my sister to pick up my money. I thought they'd get it. So it's a lot of time. I did give my breakfast. I'd get a cup of cocoa and a slice of toast. That was my breakfast. Because a lot of time for supper, I didn't get no dinner. But for supper, they'd have come in there. Well, they'd forget them out. They're sitting down on the step. There'd be nobody that many dogs. And it took them so long until sometime I just, I could hear them talking. And after a while, I could hear them quiet down. Then I'd walk back out of the teaching car and look up in there. But I'd see them dismiss the kitchen that's up in the living room, sitting down. And I said, well, they must be the forgotten man. That's what I said. They must be the forgotten man. And I sat there a little while alone. Nobody come to give me nothing eating. So I just go on back up to the hay barn. Lay on the hay and coat with sacks. And one meal would do me. Chocolates and cocoa. Chocolates and cocoa. One slice of bread. So I went through by my milking. Well, I'd catch me a cold dip of milk. A friend, Ruben, mentioned them, told me to come stay with them. Well, I told them, I said, I can't stay with you all. I said, if I stay with you, I said, I'm only getting $12 a month. Now, you got to buy your food. Now, why do you think I'm going to get money to pay you? I ain't got it. My mother sent me children to draw mine. And I don't have nothing to pay you with. So he said, we're not going to charge for nothing. I said, well, that's all right. I'll just take it as I'm finding. I slept up in those barns. That's the truth. So that's why I'm telling you, I'm in here hard. I'm in here hard.
I'm in here hard.

But that little money then, it could do you so much good when you could draw it because my mother could take that money. She didn't have to use all of that money because she could take $3 and go to the store. And she couldn't pack that food back. Couldn't pack it.
You made some money since then.
Oh, yes, sir. I made some money since then. I made plenty of money since then. But I never have got over $1.40 or $1.50 for now. That's all.
Yeah, but I mean when you go play for all these people. Oh, yes, sir.

When I go play for all these people. But you see, I just started traveling in 64. That's when you all sent me to Newport. And from that on, I went to San Francisco all back from that on into Oakland, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, New York, and overseas. Oh, I've been making good money since then. Oh, good. Yes, sir. I sure is. But at the show, I feel like I can change. Oh, yeah. Now, and making good money, if you don't know how to spend it, it won't be with you long. I wait standing on my job now. Well, they gave a raise since I been off sick. Well, I been off since Monday. You know? And the doctor, he got the time to lose before I go back to work. But they have given, we were working for $1.40, and now they give us a dime, oh, that would make $1.50 an hour. But if you go to the store with a $20 beer, you ain't got nothing. You can hang it all back. So, now, I thank God that I'm living. We belong to the end shows now, but it'll eat you up in a way. But that Benevolous, we was belong to the Benevolous Society just like he got there. We got one up there by us. But you join those Benevolous Society, it's two and a half to join. You see? And it's 25 cents a month. And that will call it, you pay 50 cents. And if someone die, you pay 50 cents.
You do.

50 cents. And if they don't die, you got paid two bits. But you could be blanched to it a hundred years, they don't get no more than that 150 dollar thing. A hundred and fifty dollars. And you'd be out of a lot of money in those societies. Oh, yeah. Now, that's all they would give you, $150. And your family got to cover the rest. It could be blanched to the Benevolous for 25 or 30 years, but you just might all them get a quarter to 50 cents a month. And I put it to the John, two and a half to John.
Yeah.
He belongs to it 30 or 50 years or something like that. You got that money out. That's all you. What happened? Okay. We got it going again.

What did I do? You're talking about Benevolous, you know. What do you want to do? It does. And the most you get is $150. When you're sick, do you get any money out of them? You get somebody, they give you about two and a half, something like that. That's the only phone that I find out, you see. That's the only one that he gets is $150. When you're sick, do you get any money out of them?

You get somebody, they give you about two and a half, something like that. That's the only phone that I find out, you see. That fellow, if he is just only by himself, that wouldn't do him no good. And suppose you had a house full of children. I want to know what could a dollar and a half do. Two and a half. That couldn't do nothing. That's all we get to. So, uh, you know. That's all we get to. That's all we get to. That's all we get to. So, I just don't know what to say about the benevolence, but it's mighty strong, benevolent society, strong what society is, excuse me, not Masonicists, you see. Now, Masonicists, it would have hit me. Well, I tell you, it's just like, I'm a Zabaptist myself, of the church. Well, I was just talking about that a few days ago. You see, when you get sick, I have been sick when I was young, pretty sick, you was praying for me, you know. And they come down, they pray for me, get down there and pray, and so, they said, well, God will hit you. All the time I know God will hit me. Here's a dime. He gave me a dime. That sister over there may say, well, I ain't got but a nickel. Here's a nickel. That may say, well, I ain't got enough, but God bless you.
What can that 15 cents do?

What can 15 cents do? 15 cents can't get a cut of the back, but now. Sure. But I tell you what, I wished a lot of time, now I can see way back days, when things were really cheap. If I'd tell you all what I have did, you wouldn't believe me. Only time was hard. You ever heard of Tucker, Pepper Grace?
Yeah.

Sure. I have eaten, but it have grown out of season. It have run like a watermelon. And around, we have picked it and boiled it. It wouldn't get done. And eat that, drink the water off it, bite the bread. But we chew that, that, uh, Pepper Grace just like we chewing a cow chew a cud. You saw a cow chew a cud. Well, that's what we have chewed. Chew a cow. Oh, yes, yes. It was too, uh, tough to chew up the swallow. So we just chew and chew until we get the juice out and then we spit that out and throw it away and bite the bread and drink some juice.
See? Uh-huh.
But we still was eating. Time was really tough.

Somebody's coming. We can, we can wait. Okay. I'm not going to turn it off again for nothing. Okay, let's see. You know, I wanted to ask you about guitar players from Bethel, uh, from Ethel and Baker and all these different places when you were growing up.

Well, uh, when I was growing up and following up these places, uh, the best guitar players that I have known in music, uh, take for Butcher, he used to play a guitar too, Phil, but he was the best and, uh, his brother Fred and, uh, Dane Jackson. Dane Jackson was great with a guitar. And dude Morgan. Uh, to my remembers, I think that was the best I heard. No more than the others that I heard that's grab a guitar and sing a little here and jump where we are, you know. And so, but I think these men's here was the best. Where were these other fellas from? Well, uh, Dane Jackson lived up there on Mr. Albert Mills' place up there in Plains. And, uh, uh, which case been here, I guess all his days, ain't he? Oh, 27.

And dude Morgan, he was down by Scotland. He played guitar in the theater. And, uh, of course, the other later guitar pickers that I met, uh, well, they, it's really good too, but they drank so much music and, uh, stopped playing the guitar and started talking and then they started back again. Such as Lee Jenkins and Robert Jenkins and, uh, Herman Johnson. I guess you know Herman Johnson. Yeah, I bet.
Great, good. Great, good.

So, and, uh, this lady, uh, they called her, uh, she, she wore her hair just like a man with a brace back, you know. Texas. They called it Texas. They had a play with Annie Allison one night and that woman could do more with a guitar and a monkey could with a coconut. She could. That woman could play in there. And so, she was there for the play that night. Henry Gaines walked in and he asked her, let me play with you. She told him, come out. She played with a bar neck on her finger just like Freddie McDowell do. Mm-hmm.
Well, that woman taking that guitar there.
Oh, my God. I don't believe a monkey could wrestle with a coconut as good as she could play that guitar. So, Henry Gaines, he got mad cause she beat him playing a guitar. Yeah, yeah.
Okay.
And, and, and want to jump on her.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah. People's up there got, uh, scared of him because he, uh, he packs a little gun, you see.
What's up, you guys, Barney? I didn't, I didn't, I didn't hear you. What about? Okay. I see you all later.
All right. All right. All right. What about, uh, did you ever hear a fella called Lacey Collins from that?

Well, me and Lacey Collins used to play together. Well, Lacey Collins learned me a lot of his notes, you see. And Lacey Collins just absolutely, he could pick a guitar. He just sat down there and put his cap over his eye. He wouldn't pat his feet or nothing. Just stretch his feet right out before him. And just, just absolutely, he didn't forget guitars, well I may say. But he really could play. He could play a guitar. But he finally, uh, died. He was a guitar player and a big gambler. And I loved his music. I believe he could play anything that he wanted to play. He played guitar and he could play piano. Yes, he played that. He was really great.
And your sister's playing piano now? Oh, yes, sir.
She playing piano and, uh, she's really can hit some good boogies on that piano.
That's Mabel Lee, will you?

Yes, sir. She, uh, plays piano now. Well, uh, I got some boys there. That boy you seen at my house today, that's my son. Robert Williams, Jr. Well, there's two of my boys, they're taking up this, uh, rock and roll. That, uh, beaters playing, uh, to keep it up, you see. So, uh, I think that's, uh, good money, uh, making tune with the playing in there, you see.
You know, I think in 1959 you told me that one of your sons was seven years old and he was a preacher. Is that the same one?

Well, down in Baton Rouge, he's preaching now. What? Yes, that's Edelie Williams. Mm-hmm. Well, he's, he's preaching. How old is he now, though? Well, he's right in eighteen now. Oh, wow. Yes, he's preaching. He's preaching. So, all the rest of my boys, uh, well, I've, only two of them here that is taking their music. And the rest of them, well, they ain't doing anything. Just, you know, playing around.
Do they, do they play with a pick or do they play with their fingers?
They, they, they pick it, you know. Pick it. Got a, got a fast tune with rock and roll stuff.
And they use their fingers or they?
Yes, use their fingers.
Oh. Yes. Well, they might learn how to play like you after they get small.

Well, uh, in my time of playing guitar, well, I had a fast chord I used to carry. But I don't care no more and I just wonder why. I don't care. I just got there. Well, it's something my tune is kind of fast. Mm-hmm. And some of them, they ain't too slow. I never play too slow. But in my playing, before, I used to have a voice. I could, I could scream. Just bring my voice down just like I want it. But this touch, the one that was so close on me, see that cuts my speech. Mm-hmm. And there's a lot of people, they used to have us to play up there. Miss, Miss Albert is out down the plank road. You know Miss Charleston store. Yeah. Well, they had a fellow up there. He was a me-mind-giving. And me, so he would be up there playing. And they'd have me. So those white folks that were before they heard me. And they just put their head down and just drop money. For me. All I had to put my hand down and me. And they said, boy, they just be dropping money in the head for me. and it had me, so those white folks said it before, who hear me, and they just put their hat down and just drop money for me. All I had to put money and receive was and they just be dropping money in the hat for me. It was sad tonight, while I was playing at it, they was coming, yes. Those white folks was coming up there while I was playing at it. I could, when I take the blues, I could just sit down and just hoop. I can't sing so good now. If they have to send me to the hospital, I'ma tell them about this, my voice, you know? Oh yeah. Yes. And then I'm gonna try to get on some blues. Take it, yes. But I'm making it pretty good, like it is. Yes, pretty good.
It's mighty good. What about your uncle?

Did he play with you? Simon Carney, yes, he was a guitar player. But the most that he played was with a knife, you see? About to sing about the gambling man, the biggest I ever heard him play, gambling man.
How does that go? I don't know.

Well, the show that he gambled all night long, and he got up and threw his car away. Now I wonder why the poor man got. That's what it sounded, yes. That's what it sounded, yes. That's what it sounded, sad. Well, I got a sister in New Orleans. She, uh, she, uh, she plays guitars. Yes. That sounds sad. Well, I got a sister in New Orleans. She plays guitars, but she don't play too much now. She got up in eights, and she always kept some of them good guitars, those Gibson, you know, that's a good guitar. That's what I always called for, a Gibson, but like I could never wake up on them. A guitar with this. A Gibson, good guitar. So, those Gibson absolutely are, can put your music down. Where does your sister live at? That's 2526 South Robinson Street.
2526, what's her name?
She's Rosalie Gibson.
25? Yes, sir.
26 South Robinson. Yes, that's right. Rosalie Gibson.
Gibson. Oh, good, huh? You know, we might find her. I hope she's still playing the guitar.
Well, she can play. She can play guitar.
Well, maybe they'll bring you back down there sometime, you know?

Well, I hope so. I enjoyed being there. You was there, wasn't you? Yeah, that time. Yes, I enjoyed being there. Y'all would really treat us nice. They're taking us to a big place and bought us some food. And what we eat. I don't know how much you pay for that food, but it really puts a lot on your plate.
Yes.

Now, this white man would take me to the place. You see, I love the whiskey then, you see. You what? I love the whiskey then. He carried me over there to eat. But after I seen all the whiskey standing on the shelf, I said, can we buy something to drink here? He said, get anything you want. I said, well, I don't want nothing to eat then. Just give me a bottle of whiskey.
Where did you play? Sir? Where did you play?
That was in the French 70s, wasn't it? French Quarter. Yes, the French Quarter. Oh, yeah. I mean, Willie B. Thomas and his wife was there, and that fella played at Harmonita. Is he from New Orleans?
Knows this fella played at Harmonita. He lived there in Baton Rouge.
Willie B. Thomas knows him well. Clyde Causey or Henry Thomas? What's that one? There's two of them.

I know that used to play with Smokey Babe on the record. Where did you want? Well, anyhow. Oh, is that guy a young student that played the Harmonica? I'm trying to remember now. Well, they had him over here at the LSU too when he was out there blowing his Harmonita too. I'm trying to remember who that is. Do you remember? I don't remember who that is. Do you remember? I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't remember.
I don't remember. Well, he's a little bit heavier than I am.
It may not be as heavy.
But that's all he plays is a harmonita. A young man? Yes, he's young. He's very good with that harmonita.
Have you ever played harmonita?
Yes, I used to play harmonica a great bit before my tonsils got too bad.
Can't play it now.

I used to play a harmonica a great bit before my tonsils got too bad. Couldn't play it now. And I've been thinking about just going, give me a rack, and put my music in with a harmonica to save me a singing, you know. Every once in a while I sing. So that's what I'm figuring on down. I had a harmonica when I was over in Los Angeles. No, not there I was. Yeah. I was in Los Angeles. I believe it was. See, now I don't want to get it. I was. But Junior Welch, he wanted it, and I let him have it. Yes. Joe Turner, he lives in New Orleans too. He was overseas with us.
I never see him down there. I see him in New York once in a while, but I never see him in New Orleans.

Well, they was making cars off and cross the sea back over here, and them cars coming back to them $50 and $60. They must have thought they got to be cheap, but I'm telling you, they was having spells behind it. Yeah. But they had to pay. But I never have called back nine times that I left home. All I did is get someone to write me a letter. Well, it's one thing about me. I can't read, I write.
They treat you right in Europe when you're over there?

Yes, they treat me just as fine. I didn't know I was knowing all the way from Europe, all the way through into East Germany. I go on the stage there and come out. The men and the ladies say, Robert P. to call my name better than I could call her. They say, we've been great laying off the sea. Now we see all my pictures, my records and everything. So when we come out from playing, they would just carry us over to the house and fix a big dinner for us. Let us drink and sit down and eat. And there's some folks when I was playing in Oakland, there's some folks from New Orleans, was in Oakland. And this white man, he got him, he said, you have changed your music a whole lot different. He said, yeah, there wasn't nothing. He said, but this year what you're playing now is really great. Well, I told him, no, so I said, we ought to be sitting down there playing that music behind all them convicts. And I was one, too. He said, I was looking any time maybe to get a knife in my back, he said, you can't trust them people up there. Well, he had to laugh. He said, well, I don't much blame you. Well, it was kind of dangerous up there, you know. Any kind of prison is dangerous. Yes. So, but I'm just so glad I'm from up there that I don't know what to do.
Well, we're about to run out of tape now. So, I'm sure to thank you all for giving me your history.
Well, you're really welcome.
I know those students will want to hear it, you know, and want to learn about this kind of music. Maybe some of them will even learn how to play it someday.
Oh, yes.
I hope so. I know your vehicle.

Well, I have met a lot of white folks that really likes the blues. There's a lot of them that I left tapes up there with when I was in Oakland, California. And when I left them overseas, a couple of the white folks, one, well, I left them some tapes. They blew. I said, you want to learn this shit? I said, yes, sit down and take your time. I got to play too fast and I play slow and you learn these blues. And they took them. I give music lessons over there in Oakland. White man that I was staying with, well, he just let me have went on. And he was chatting and it was down, no, two and a half.

Let's see. We're now at Butch Cage's house, huh? Where we at exactly? Zachary, yeah. Zachary, Lewis, yeah. And the number here is? 5131 Old Slaughter Road. 5131 Old Slaughter Road. And what's today's date? It's May the... 13th. 13th. 13th. 13th? May the 13th, 1967. What is your name anyhow? James Cage. And what do they call you? Butch.
How come they call you Butch anyhow? I don't know. Mama called me that nickname.
Nickname. Nickname. They've been calling you that since you were a little boy? Yes, sir. I see. I can hear myself talk. Oh, that's terrible. It sounds awful.
I don't want them either. I'm so tall.

It's so funny when you hear yourself talk on one of those things. It's just a little bit later, you know. It makes me nervous, I swear. Anyhow, where were you born at? I was born in Franklin County, Mississippi. Franklin County, Mississippi. What's the nearest town? Hamboys. Matthews was in the nearest big town. Yeah, but that's Adams, isn't it? Adams County. Yeah, it's in Mississippi, yeah. Yeah, that's to the west, I believe, frankly. Hamboys was made from Mississippi. Oh, yeah. And what year were you born? 1894. Remember the exact day? Well, May. No, not that exact day, but in May. In May. Well, happy birthday. Yeah. I used to say the 16th. I used to use that, but I wasn't sure of it. Well, you got three days to go, isn't it? Yes. Anyhow, what kind of music did you hear out there when you were growing up? I had a drum. Go get my wife. Oh, you got a wife still? Yes.
Well, we're going to have a field band. Yes. Yes. Well, did your family play music? Yes. I had a sister. Two sisters to play accordion. And one brother.

Mm-hmm. And my brother. I got another brother play. Your mom and your daddy, your uncles, your grandfather, or grandmother play? Oh, hell no. She was a dancer. Which one? My mama. Oh, yeah? What kind of dancing did she do? All time, you know. Well, I suppose so. She was the best in Franklin County. What kind was she doing? What did she do? Did she do the buck and wing? The whole thing. I saw her. She's done all kinds. Well, that's before my time. I don't know what you mean by old time dancing. I never saw it. You know, I just wondered if they had a name for it. Oh, yeah. You think? Swing out or something? Swing out or something. Swing out?
They didn't have no special name because she could do any kind of stuff. Oh, yeah. Soft shoe?
Yes. Shine shoe, too. Now, I say, did she do that soft shoe dancing? Yes. You understand? Yes.
Did she dance on a stage or...? No, ma'am. We didn't have no stage. It's just around, huh? Where did you dance at?
Yeah. And the ball was. Where the what? And the what the ball would be. Oh, they had balls.
They had balls. Yeah. They had balls at the people's house, wasn't it?

Oh, yeah. I just wondered if she danced in the yard ever, you know? I sometimes see people do buck and wing in the yard. Well, they did how that dance. Did you ever do any quadrilles or reels or mazarkas or anything like that? Or polkas?
Well, see, I guess it's not exactly. I don't think.
Did they call the dancers? You know, they have a guy tell you what? Yes. Oh, what would he call? Figure garter. Yeah, what kind of figures did they have then in those times?
They had from four and these that you could dance with. And from that time, from eight to sixteen, from sixteen to three to two.
And they danced around and they were swing partners. They used to swing partners. Did they have Dozy Do then? What's that? Did they ever hear Dozy Do? That's what the hillbillies call it, you know?
I don't know about it. The old man swung his partner. Oh, yeah. The old man swung his partner. Had a figure corner. Oh, yeah.
What kind of music did they use?
Any kind. Oh, Phyllis Lavey.
Yeah. Drums. What songs would they play to dance to? What songs would they play to dance to? At these dances? Yankadoodl.
Yankadoodl.
Yeah. Old Greek dance. Yeah. What other one? Dixie. Yeah. They would play, you know, blues things to dance to?
Yeah, man. Yeah, man. All kinds. All kinds. What kind of fife is that you got there? I don't know what known it is. Mr. Hadley gave me this fife. Oh, that's not a homemade one, I don't guess.
No, sir.
Oh, good. I can't play it now.
Was that the kind of fife you had when you were a little boy?
Yes, sir. I used to make them out of cane.
Mm-hmm. And did you... I wasn't able to find that. Let me see. Did you blow it like this in front of your... No, no, sir. You always held it this way.
Yeah, you could have some, you blow like this.

Oh, the end blown type, you think? Some of them. Some of them. But you never did have that kind. No. You had the cross-blown. Yes, sir. Cross-blown right there. Yes. Oh, yeah. And y'all had drums too? Yes, sir. What'd they make the drums out of?
It would be a drum that like these drums they got now.
Oh, a made drum. Not a homemade drum, but a bought drum. Yes.
What'd they have to get a drum and a bass drum and a quiet? Mm-hmm.

If you used to go out and get under the tree and have... Picnics, they call them. Mm-hmm. Yes. And what would you play then? I'd play anything like old Mockingbird. Oh, Mockingbird? Listen to the Mockingbird? Yes.

Can you play that now? Oh, I can't make the fire say that now. I used to play a mockingbird. I can't play it now. I can't play it now. I thought we need to practice up a little bit. Yeah, I need to practice up. I have to keep moving. I used to play love somebody. Yeah. How do the words go? How do the words go? I got play now.
You probably need to practice up a little bit.
Yeah, I need to practice up. I have to keep moving. I used to play Love Somebody.
Love Somebody? I don't know what that is. That's a two or four time piece. How do the words go? Remember any of the words?
No, I wouldn't know the words. But that's not a sound. Oh, yeah.
Can you make it on that? I guess not. Okay, make it safe. I think it's time to dance to.
Yeah, yeah. Let me see. You had dance halls in? You danced in the floor of somebody's house? Or in a big hall?
On the tree sometime in that house sometime. On the naked ground?
On the naked ground?
Yes, I would march around with the drum. Mm-hmm. And I had the people falling.
Yes. Well, how long did you live out there in Mississippi, in Franklin County? Were you a big boy?
My children frightened in Franklin County until 1919.
You didn't have to go to the war?
I was exempted from the war.
I had two children. Oh, I see. Yes. So, where did you go in 1919?
I moved. Meadville got wet out. Got my house wet up and two of my children. Mm. Then I come on down here and do that in 1920.
In 1927. In 1927, you say anything?
In 1927. No, I went to Mr. John Downey.
Oh, yeah, that was in 1921, wasn't it? Oh, you left in 1921. Yeah, 1921.
You left which place? I left. Lindsay. Lindsay.

Now, I thought you'd worry me. I left Meadville, Mississippi. And come to the slaughter of Louisiana. And from Florida to Lindsay. And then from Lindsay? And from Lindsay. I went back to Mississippi and stayed until 1927. I ran off from Lindsay.
What do you mean, run off?

I was on a hard task, Natchez. Oh, yeah. And I got tired of it and I slipped off of my back. And 22, I was in Natchez, Mississippi. And then 23, I was in Natchez. And then 24, I was in Bad, Mississippi. I'd move every year, you know. Well, they didn't catch you then. And I moved from Fair to Port Gibson. And I lived there in Mentecetal, Mississippi. And stayed my long desire to fix for you.
Did you ever know any Wolcotts in Port Gibson?
I know of Mr. Charlie Humphers.

And Mr. Ryan Humphers. Did they have that minstrel show? It seems to me the people in Port Gibson had that rabbit foot show. Did you ever see the rabbit? They did. Yeah. They did. Who was that? Oh, I don't know if they had...
You didn't know those people? Well, no. Well, I remember the rabbit foot show had two of them. Yeah.
Well, Wolcott is the one I'm talking about. Wolcott had one. I don't know if he had two, but I know he had one.
Well, there's nothing there, too. You called Snowball or something like that.
You like minstrel shows?
Yeah, I used to like them. He'd tell the televisions going on now and I could tell the video.
Oh, of course.
That's the place. Yeah.
It's cheaper, too. Yeah. You don't have to pay anything for a television. That's right. Except when it breaks. Yes, sir. Well...
Then I come...
I've been here...

I come here back in 27 and been here ever since. And you've been in this same house for how long? I built this house. About... About 44 I moved in here. Before I ever came to Louisiana? Yes, sir. Yes, sir. That was...
I didn't come here until like... Well, I moved in here.
Well I moved in there. I've been here 20 some years.
Where did you take up the fiddle? Where did you first start playing the fiddle?
Oh man, Cal Williams. He used to be a fiddle player and Frank Felters.
Cal Williams and Frank Felters?
Yeah. And I learned from them. Where was that? That was all around there. I was talking about Franklin County. Franklin County. Yeah. And Jefferson.
And did they have many guitar pickers out there? No, not many. I thought they'd have plenty of guitar pickers. Is that in the Delta or on the edge? That's hills, huh?
Oh no, that's just around there. That's 21 miles east of Matthew.
So that's hills then, huh? Yes, sir. Yes. You have to work hard out there? No, I wouldn't like for nobody. Work for yourself or just not work? Well, didn't work.

How'd you live if you didn't work? Well, my papa died when I was 10 years old. Oh, I see. And I worked six months for a dollar a month and paid six dollars on his coffin. His coffin cost $11. A sharpshooter. What's the shop you? What's the shop you doing? That little old shop coffin made like a big up here and little old back down there. Just like that don't make them now.
Big up at the top and strong at the bottom. Yeah.
Yeah. Cost $11. Now I worked six months and paid a dollar a month. And my boy. Did you? Did you? Did you? Then mama gave me away three times.
Your mama gave you away three times? She went on and ran off. Yeah.
She wasn't able to take care of her. Yeah. Well, that must have been hard on you. Oh, it was. I got on pretty good because I was always staying with somebody, you know.

I'd run off when I got ready. Were you playing any music then? Were you playing your fiddle? Playing any okay in five. They didn't pay you to do that I bet, huh? No, no sir. They didn't care if you never played. You didn't make a nickel? A penny?
No, I worked six months for $6.
No, I mean playing the five.
Oh, I'd get two, three dollars maybe. One dollar or something like that a night. They didn't pay nobody much.
Well, I guess you could buy quite a bit with a dollar out there. Oh, yes sir. In those times.
I remember when I married in 1913. I got a battle of life for $5. I was on the railroad then.
You worked on the railroad?
Oh, yes sir.
What did you do?
Shuffled tied and pulled out old tied and put in good on tamper tied. You know what tamper is, don't you?

I do. Yeah. Oh well. Did you have to sing along with that? Yeah, I saw you had a song go with it. What kind of song would go with it? What kind of song would go with it? Do you remember any of the words? Oh no, I can't sing them, no. Well just sing them if you can't sing them. Let me see.
When you hear my bulldog barking. When they bark somebody round. Somebody round. And you hit, you tap every time. When you hear my bulldog barking somebody round.
And you tap when you say round. Yeah, you'd be whacking.
Mm-hmm. And that's the thing.
I come through a hard place. You come through a hard? Yes sir. A hard place? Oh yes sir. I was full. Yes sir. Well that's hard work, I know.
I watched them. I never had to tamp tires or line track.
I did the wrong jack. You know jack it up and down. I was a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of bamboo
bamboo I line track, when I get out of line, I took a bar and put on that, a whole lot of, and

then so I keep on doing that till I throw it back. And you sang when you did that too? Yes sir. Remember what you sang when you line track? Well sir, I don't remember, if I could sing I'd do it. But a song with it. You could just say the words. You could just say the words if you remember the words. Well it doesn't use anything. I know a friend of mine used to work on the tracks, when I line them he'd say, Peaches and Cream, Rock and Raw. You ever hear that one? No sir. Peaches and Cream, Rock and Raw, you can line them if you try. Yeah. And they got, Captain Can't Read, Captain Can't Write, how he's gonna know when the tracks line right.

We used to say, nigga lick glasses. Lick em all the pants, but when a white man lick em he lick em all his hands. All his pants, that's right. We used to sing that. Nigga lick glasses. I never heard that. I never heard that. I was hanging and the white man lick em all the pants. We used to sing behind him, be whacking, you know. Yeah. Yeah.

Did you ever know an old, old song, I think maybe it was a fiddle piece called down in Shinbone Alley? I know an Arkansas traveler. Oh you know an Arkansas traveler? I thought old time. Yeah. I like that one. I used to try to play that. There's a lot of numbers I like. I like
songs. Leather, leather bridges. See that was all that go there. What's that? Leather britches.

Oh, leather britches. Yeah. And Arkansas traveler. Yellow jacket. Yellow jacket. Yeah. And uh, did you ever know Soldiers Joy? No, I thought. That's more of a hillbilly number I guess. Yeah. That's too new for me. Yeah. Well I know you did a lot of them. I wrote some things down I wanted to, to ask you. What kind of work did your father do?
He worked on a farm. Clean up, uh, made cotton and corn. Was he a sharecropper? Uh, no he wasn't out. We had plenty of sharecroppers. He didn't.

He didn't, he didn't do that. No. Yeah. Did you ever hear of a man called Stack of Dollars? Oh yes I did. Well who was Stack of Dollars? I never didn't know much about him. Oh I don't know him but I heard of him. Stack of Dollars. What about Stack of Lee? Did you ever know him? I used to play that. You used to play Stack of Lee? I don't know him no. They say he was a real man. Say did you ever see Billy Cressans? No. He used to put a whole cup and sauce in his mouth and all that. I think he, he played around here in Donaldsonville. What, what did he play? He was a, he was in minstrel shows, in those tent shows. Oh, I know this thing. What happened to, to, to Clarence and Cornelius Edwards? You know them? No. Two brothers? Guitar players? No, no I don't know them. I think they're from right here in Zachary and they were at your house when I was here before.
Oh, I know who you're talking about. You know what, Clarence and now they say in Alson, don't you?
They, they in Alson down there always got to me down Scotland on 61.
What is the name of the town? Alson. Alson. Alson. Alson.
You know, I'm here in where? Scotlandville. Scotlandville.
Yeah, Alson.
Alson, just like 61.
You go, you hit 61 and bring it right down to Alson.
And their name is, is Clarence and Cornelius what? Yeah.
What the, what the, Edmund wasn't it?
They said Edmund. They was Edmund, and Papa was Edmund. Yeah. The father was Edmund. Yeah, that's fine. And so that was their name too, Edmund.
Did you ever belong to church?
Yeah, I belonged to the sanctified church.

Oh, you're sanctified now? No, I ain't. I ain't got out. You got out, but you were sanctified. Yeah. Did you ever play your, your fiddling church or your guitar? Yeah, I saw. No, not the biggest place I played. Which, which did you play? Which box did you play in church? Your guitar or your fiddle? I played my fiddle.
I had another partner play my guitar.
Ed Straughan is a preacher. He lived near now. He had a church he played. He got off. Come on in.

Let's, let's cut it off for a minute so you can get a little beer. That might be good for your throat, huh? I think they're out there. Yeah, I think it's working now. We're talking about in church you used to play. I used to play. Remember that hall point up in Edmonton, Mississippi? Jefferson Hall. Well, I know about that. I never was there. I heard of Walter Barnes and a friend of mine used to play with Walter Barnes, but he wasn't there that night and I thank the Lord for that. Oh, that's good.
Well, about 250 people got put up in there and I got mad in there in 1919. My first wife died. You know that song about that? You know they had a song about that? No, I never did know it.
Well, they had one about called the death of Walter Barnes and they had one called, wasn't that an awful day in Natchez?
Yeah, well that's the place I'm at now. I belong to that church. I stayed there I don't know how long. I was baptized in the Mississippi River there.
And tell me about baptism. Do people sing at baptisms when they put you in the water?

They talk to you. You know the preacher get up and talk about it. You know the preacher, you're baptized according to your fashion. In the name of the father and son all the way. Then they put you in.
Well I thought they had some songs that sang it when you were there. Oh they do sing.
That's a, I can't sing it all now.
Do you ever remember that song about under the bamboo tree? No sir. If you like a me like I like a you. Oh I know that. That's a. That's the one I'm talking about. Oh yeah sir. I know it.
I'll play that sometimes.
Oh my God's back the ice. Well don't worry. Yeah you might like it better with the ice. Okay thank you.
Now I got everything but the drink. Oh.
How long can you put me in the drink?

Never mind she's got it. Did you ever go to any quilting parties? What guy? A quilting party like they'd be making a quilt. Oh yeah sir. Well what went on at that? I've heard about them but I never was at one.
They'd have coffee and tea cakes and singing.
I thought they had a certain round of coffee. And would you play your fiddle there or no? Sometimes yeah sometimes I would play. Would the people pat?
No I didn't pat then.
They just sang. Uh. Uh huh.
Yeah sir. They had quilting. My mama used to quilt all the time.
Well I've heard songs about that but I've never been to a quilting party. I never knew exactly what went on. They don't make me anymore. They buy blankets. Yeah they buy.
Oh you don't drink this, eh Pete? No you don't. Oh you got it.

Did you ever go to these meetings where they have fiddlers and they all meet up and see which one can play? I know I have a pass yet. You never did? No. You don't try to cut him a new frock as they call it? I have one that come in there when I dance and try to play at me. Uh huh. But I'm lucky enough to beat them out. In New Orleans sometimes they'll have a couple of bands get together. And the one that wins gets a cup.
Yeah. Have you ever seen him get a silver cup for anything like that? No. No. No. No.
We didn't get that at that time.
They ain't gonna cheap you know.
Oh yeah. Yeah. Did you ever go to Westerfield? No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
No.
No. No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.

No. Did they do that up in Mississippi and different places in Louisiana? Yes, they do that. It wasn't why I didn't do that. Just come to each other's house. Not much, though, but they used to do it again. Who were some of the good musicians you knew like that?
Oh, man, Cal Williams.
And that's from Franklin County, huh?
Frank Felters.
And who else did you know?
I know a whole lot of the Felters used to play a guitar. Joe Felters, Artie Felters. A whole lot of them used to play a guitar.
What about around Natchez? I wasn't talking about all from Natchez.
They're on Staffly. You know where that is, no? Mm-mm. Staffly Station.
No, I'm not too familiar. I've just been to Natchez one time.
Well, they got a branch from Natchez to Jackson. Mm-mm. Let me get on to Jackson's branch and stuff.
Mm-mm. That's Staffly. Did you ever hear of a Coon John? I did. I am, but I don't know much about it. I don't either. What is it? It's a kind of a rhythm. I think a dance and a rhythm.
Oh.
They used to play on the piano sometimes. You know. And what about waltzes? You play many waltzes? Yeah, I know. That's a lot of them. What are some of the waltzes you play?
I used to play over the way. I play a hip-hop, but I don't know what it was. Mm-mm. I just play my song.
Mm-mm. Oh, the wave of one. Well, since I came here with Dr. Oster, you done some traveling, huh?
Yes, I did. I went back once. I went to Manhattan. To Manhattan? Yes. I went from down to Philadelphia.
Mm-mm. Weren't you up at Newport, too? Newport and Boston, too.
Mm-mm. I had my first trip. Oh, you made several trips, huh? Yes. If I found out I couldn't do nothing, then they left me alone. Mm-mm. Mm-mm. You went twice, didn't you?
You went in 61 and 62. Mm-mm.
I know one time you went with Willie B. Did you go to...
Both times he went.
Both times with Willie B.? Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Did you hear any good fiddle players up there?

North of the city, I went to Newport. They had plenty of them up there. Mm-mm. They had one from Canada. Canada, Connecticut, whatever they call that place. Connecticut. Yes. You know his name? No, sir. I don't know his name.
He can play good.
Mm-mm.
Yes. And what about, uh, let's see, uh, guitar players? Did you hear any good guitar players? Yeah, I saw on the stage. What? Uh-huh.
There was not many violin players.
But a few, some guitar players. Yeah.
That white fella that played, he'd jump them.
Kennedy, did you hear that?

Yeah, but I ain't talking about him. That's another time. Oh, this man hasn't been. He called you the Mexican or something. Mm-hmm. And he could play good. He was a good guy. He's about the best man. And he had plenty of songs.
Oh, plenty of songs. Yeah. I guess you might have learned some new songs. What about that?
Well, I'll forget them. I'm too old now to learn them.
Well, the old songs are the best anyway, aren't they?
Yes, sir.
But the young people lose this year. Oh, they know that stuff. That old song too. How old were you when you took out pedals?
Oh, it started in 1911. Mm-hmm .

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: Cage recalls a slavery-time song his mother sang
segments.summary: Cage recites a song his mother used to sing, a racist slavery-time verse; the interviewer says it must date from slavery.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: Cutting sugar cane near Smithfield and Napoleonville
segments.summary: Cage says he was a poor cane cutter who would sometimes sing; he worked at Smithfield across the river from Baton Rouge and at Napoleonville, and kept ahead of the cutters behind him.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: The song 'You Don't Know My Mind'
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about the first song Cage played; Cage names it 'You Don't Know My Mind' and says he played it all the time.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: Early music boxes, records and 'Bill Bailey'
segments.summary: Cage had no music box growing up, only a cylinder-type one; they trade bits of 'Why Don't You Come Home, Bill Bailey' and 'Babe, Please Don't Let Me Fall'.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: Listening to Blind Lemon Jefferson and Bessie Smith records
segments.summary: Cage says he listened to all the blues singers on record, naming Blind Lemon Jefferson and Bessie Smith; the interviewer keeps their records.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: Ma Rainey, Memphis Minnie and a woman's blues song
segments.summary: Cage recalls Ma Rainey, seen or confused with another singer, and recites a blues about a woman whose man has left; the interviewer mentions Bessie Smith at Newport and Punch Miller playing the song.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: Cage's family: dancer mother and musical siblings
segments.summary: Cage says his mother was a dancer, his father was not, and siblings played accordion; his brother Fred played guitar and a son plays guitar in Syracuse.

segments.chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
segments.title: No brass bands in the country; bands in town
segments.summary: Cage says there were no trumpets or bands where he grew up except drums, and white people had the marching bands in Meadville and Natchez.

segments.chapter: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
segments.title: Drums beaten at funerals
segments.summary: Cage says drums were played at funerals, on the way to the cemetery and back.

segments.chapter: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
segments.title: Benevolent society dues and sick benefits
segments.summary: Cage and the interviewer discuss the benevolent society across the street: $2.50 a week sick pay, 50 cents levied when a member dies.

segments.chapter: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
segments.title: When fife and drum funeral music was heard
segments.summary: Cage dates the funeral drumming to 1905-1909, with fife and drums, and the interviewer asks what tunes were played.

segments.chapter: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
segments.title: Will young players take up old-time fiddling
segments.summary: The interviewer asks whether youngsters will play Cage's kind of fiddle music; Cage says not many.

segments.chapter: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
segments.title: Everyone's names recorded for the tape; young people prefer new music
segments.summary: The interviewer gets names from all present for the record, including Robert Pete Williams and Dick Allen, and notes nobody else plays old-time fiddle locally; Cage says youngsters do not play his kind.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Williams on picking style and tunings
segments.summary: Williams says he picks with two right-hand fingers and uses all of his left, and plays in C, flat E minor and Spanish tunings, sometimes with a knife; cross-note is flat E minor.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Williams's influences and how he began playing
segments.summary: Williams says he played like Lightning Hopkins and modelled his music on Blind Lemon Jefferson; he started around age 34 after watching Bush Keyes play at suppers.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Williams buys his first guitar for four dollars
segments.summary: Asked where he was born, Williams says Zachary, and tells how a white woman sold him her son's guitar for $4 after he failed with a cheap first one.
