segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Country suppers, quitting the blues, then prison, the dairy and release to Mr. Eastley
segments.summary: In one long monologue Williams describes playing suppers and white parties, giving up the blues for church, prison captains who loved his playing, work at the dairy and with dogs, and being taken by Rudolph Eastley.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Reel change to the third reel
segments.summary: Mrs. Cage interjects while the tape is changed and the interviewer announces the third reel with Cage and Williams.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Williams's vision while on guard post at the prison
segments.summary: Williams tells how, while on guard duty, something touched his shoulder and told him he would be home for Christmas; he prayed and felt relieved.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
segments.title: Release to Rudolph Eastley, the governor, and giving up playing for suppers
segments.summary: Williams tells how Eastley took him from camp to his place above Zachary, where he played for the governor, and why he now declines to play out; he recalls 1932 wages.

segments.chapter: Williams on hard times and money
segments.title: Williams's hard childhood, welfare and raising his siblings
segments.summary: Williams describes walking with his mother to the welfare office, a $12 monthly job, sleeping in barns, and raising his siblings without a father.

segments.chapter: Williams on hard times and money
segments.title: Money earned since touring began in 1964
segments.summary: Williams says he earned good money since Newport in 1964, then travelling to San Francisco, New York and overseas, though he still earns $1.40 an hour at his job.

segments.chapter: Williams on hard times and money
segments.title: Benevolent societies pay little
segments.summary: Williams explains society dues and the $150 maximum payout, and describes his Baptist church's collections for the sick.

segments.chapter: Williams on hard times and money
segments.title: Eating pepper grass in hard times
segments.summary: Williams recalls chewing tough pepper grass for its juice when food was scarce.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: The best guitar players around Baker and Zachary
segments.summary: Asked about local guitarists, Williams names Butch Cage, his brother Fred, Dane Jackson and Dude Morgan, then Lee and Robert Jenkins and Herman Johnson.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: A woman guitarist who outplayed Henry Gaines
segments.summary: Williams tells of a woman guitarist who played with a bar on her finger and beat Henry Gaines, who then wanted to attack her.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Lacey Collins
segments.summary: Williams says he played with Lacey Collins, who taught him notes and played guitar and piano; Collins died, a gambler.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Williams's sister and sons who play music
segments.summary: Williams says his sister plays boogie piano, two sons play rock and roll, and another son is a preacher in Baton Rouge.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Williams's voice and white audiences passing the hat
segments.summary: Williams says his voice has weakened, and recalls playing for white folks who dropped money in a hat.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Uncle Simon Carney and sister Rosalie Gibson
segments.summary: Williams says his uncle Simon Carney played with a knife and sang about a gambling man, and gives the address of his guitar-playing sister in New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Williams's New Orleans visit and the French Quarter
segments.summary: Williams recalls being treated well in New Orleans and playing in the French Quarter with Willie B. Thomas.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Harmonica players and Williams giving up harmonica
segments.summary: They discuss a young harmonica player; Williams says he used to play harmonica until his tonsils got bad and gave one away to Junior Welch.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Touring Europe and being recognised by fans
segments.summary: Williams says he was treated fine in Europe, including East Germany, where fans knew his records, and tells of an Oakland audience that asked about the prison.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Closing thanks and hope that students will learn the music
segments.summary: The interviewer thanks them as the tape runs out and hopes students will learn the music.

segments.chapter: Williams on guitarists, family and touring
segments.title: Williams leaves tapes and gives lessons to white fans
segments.summary: Williams says many white people like the blues; he left tapes and gave lessons in Oakland.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Opening: location, date and Cage's name
segments.summary: The interviewer establishes they are at Cage's house in Zachary on May 13, 1967; Cage gives his name as James Cage, called Butch.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Cage's birth in Franklin County and early music
segments.summary: Cage says he was born in 1894 in Franklin County, Mississippi, and recalls a field band and his siblings playing accordion.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Cage's mother, a dancer
segments.summary: Cage says his mother danced all kinds of dances at house balls and was the best in the county.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Square dance calls and dance tunes
segments.summary: Cage describes figures and calling, partners swinging, and tunes such as Yankee Doodle and Dixie.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Cage's fife and drums
segments.summary: Cage shows a fife given to him; he used to make fifes from cane, played the cross-blown type, and had bought drums.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Picnics and tunes like 'Mockingbird' and 'Love Somebody'
segments.summary: Cage recalls playing at picnics, including 'Listen to the Mockingbird', and says he marched around with a drum.

segments.chapter: Cage's origins and Mississippi youth
segments.title: Moving from Mississippi to Louisiana and back, 1919-1927
segments.summary: Cage lived in Franklin County until 1919, was exempted from the war, moved to Louisiana and ran off from hard work, and moved around Mississippi each year until returning in 1927.

segments.chapter: Cage in Louisiana, minstrels and learning fiddle
segments.title: Rabbit Foot minstrel show at Port Gibson
segments.summary: Asked about the Wolcott minstrel show in Port Gibson, Cage remembers the Rabbit Foot shows and liked minstrels; the talk turns to television.

segments.chapter: Cage in Louisiana, minstrels and learning fiddle
segments.title: Building his house at Zachary
segments.summary: Cage says he came back in 1927 and has lived in the house he built since about 1944.

segments.chapter: Cage in Louisiana, minstrels and learning fiddle
segments.title: Learning fiddle from Cal Williams and Frank Felters
segments.summary: Cage learned fiddle from Cal Williams and Frank Felters in Franklin County and Jefferson County, where guitarists were scarce.

segments.chapter: Cage in Louisiana, minstrels and learning fiddle
segments.title: Father's death and mother giving him away
segments.summary: Cage's father died when he was 10; he worked six months to pay on the coffin, and his mother gave him away three times.

segments.chapter: Cage in Louisiana, minstrels and learning fiddle
segments.title: Pay for playing fife and fiddle
segments.summary: Cage says he earned two or three dollars a night for playing, since nobody paid much.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Railroad section work
segments.summary: Cage says he married in 1913 and worked on the railroad, tamping ties.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Railroad work songs
segments.summary: Cage sings a tamping song about a bulldog barking and a line-track chant; the interviewer offers 'Peaches and Cream'.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Old-time fiddle tunes
segments.summary: They talk about tunes such as Arkansas Traveler and Leather Britches, which Cage knows.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Stack o' Lee, minstrel performers and the Edwards brothers
segments.summary: Cage says his father farmed but was not a sharecropper; the interviewer asks about Stack o' Lee, Billy Cressans and two guitarists, Clarence and Cornelius, living near Scotlandville.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Playing in the sanctified church
segments.summary: Cage belonged to the sanctified church and played his fiddle there while a partner played guitar.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: The Natchez dance hall fire and Cage's first wife
segments.summary: They discuss the fatal fire in Natchez, which Cage says was 1919, when his first wife died.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Baptism and 'Under the Bamboo Tree'
segments.summary: Cage describes being baptised in the Mississippi River, and recalls 'Under the Bamboo Tree'.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Quilting parties
segments.summary: Cage describes quilting parties with coffee, tea cakes and singing, at which he sometimes played fiddle.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Fiddlers' contests
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about contests; Cage says he beat other players but never won a cup.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Good musicians he knew: Cal Williams and the Felters
segments.summary: Cage names Cal Williams, Frank, Joe and Artie Felters, near Staffly Station.

segments.chapter: Cage on work songs, church and social life
segments.title: Coon John rhythm and waltzes
segments.summary: Cage knows a little about Coon John and plays some waltzes.

segments.chapter: Cage on musicians, travels and old songs
segments.title: Trips to Newport, Boston, Philadelphia and New York
segments.summary: Cage describes his travel with Dr. Oster, with Willie B. Thomas, in 1961 and 1962.

segments.chapter: Cage on musicians, travels and old songs
segments.title: Fiddlers and guitarists heard at Newport
segments.summary: Cage says few fiddlers were at Newport, one from Connecticut, and a good white guitarist.

segments.chapter: Cage on musicians, travels and old songs
segments.title: Old songs and starting out in 1911
segments.summary: Cage says he is too old to learn new songs; he started in 1911.
